newsitem.title: USA: Fed keeps interest rates on steady course.
newsitem.headline: Fed keeps interest rates on steady course.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve opted on Tuesday to hold interest rates steady at its last policy-making meeting of the year.

The decision, which had been widely expected, left the key federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans at 5.25 percent and the discount rate that the Fed charges banks for money at 5 percent.
"The Federal Open Market Committee meeting ended at 12:40 p.m. (1740 GMT)," central bank spokesman Joseph Coyne said. "There is no further announcement."
Analysts are divided over the outlook for rates in 1997, though few see any pressing need for the central bank's policy-making panel to change rates soon. The committee next meets on Feb. 4-5.
Recent statistics have portrayed an economy with pockets of weakness and strength that remains surprisingly free of any inflationary tendencies after 5-1/2 years of expansion.
After stripping out volatile food and energy costs, consumer prices rose at a modest year-on-year rate of 2.6 percent in November.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan earlier this month called inflation "low," although he added that its future course remained uncertain.

Labour markets are tight and unemployment low, raising the risk of stepped-up wage demands. But product markets are, in Greenspan's words, "comfortable," indicating no shortages that could lead to higher prices.
After cutting rates by a quarter percentage point in January, the Fed has held policy steady as economic growth has first waxed and then waned.
Analysts said its next move will depend on the course that the economy takes in the new year.

If the economy starts growing much faster than its presumed long-term cruising speed of roughly 2.25 percent, the Fed is likely to raise rates. Growth much slower than that would make a rate cut more likely.
The economy expanded by 2 percent in the third quarter. Growth in the current quarter is expected to be better than that, helped by a pick-up in consumer spending in the run-up to Christmas.
The steady Fed stance does not mean that policy-makers, who are paid to worry about the economy, have no concerns.
Some fret that Wall Street stock prices may be too high. Others worry that unemployment may be too low. But none seem concerned enough to alter policy anytime soon.

Greenspan warned earlier this month that the Fed needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infected stock and other asset markets because of the risk of a subsequent crash that could damage the economy.
Some of the froth though has gone out of the stock market since then, as investors have cashed in part of their profits, pushing equity prices lower.
The Fed chairman also has his eyes on the tight labour market for signs of stepped-up wage demands that could lead to higher inflation. So far, however, that has not proved to be the case.
The unemployment rate rose to 5.4 percent in November, from 5.2 percent in October, easing some of the pressures in the labour market.
But it is still somewhat below the 5.5 percent to 5.75 percent level that some Fed officials believe is sustainable on a long-term basis without spurring inflation.
